And I think the combination of seeing, like, the infrastructure could maybe, like get a push from somewhere, or, like, be a little bit more streamlined in some way, and the fact that, you know, we really wanted to show the diversity of the African music landscape, I suppose, or the Afro-diasporic landscape, I think really from that it grew, and so it turned into workshops, a lot of, like, DJ workshops with beginning DJs that, in the end, then became, like, residents, or started playing themselves.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: We do a lot of community initiatives. This summer, we built a sound system with Adidas in Berlin, where it was really like a sound system workshop. We invited sound systems from all over the world.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: We made a documentary, I actually did that together with a resident from Oroko, from Kumasi, Project Kumasi. We made a documentary about visa inequality, so how are artists actually affected by… Any given, you know. Right, but how are they affected by, like, visa inequality? And they are very much affected.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: So we don't only want to make parties, we also want to research things, we want to archive things, we want to talk about issues that are important, we want to make sure that we give opportunities to people. So by just calling it a radio station, we just kind of want to step away from that, because that's, like, the way that we're able to archive, the way that we're able to showcase all this talent, but it's not all we do. Yeah.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, totally. It's been really interesting watching this community grow, and not even… I don't know, saying it that way also feels like I'm placing myself at the beginning of this story, but not at all. Like, I first encountered Oroko maybe 3 years ago or so, Kike had been in Nairobi giving a talk, and, like, it was just the whole point was to uplift people, and it wasn't necessarily to say, like, hey, you should submit so that you can come and show on our platform, and we can benefit from that. Instead, it's like, here are the tools that you can use to advance, whether you want to work with us or not, you know? And so, something I really…

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: But you've kind of been there for a long time. You say you haven't been there from the beginning, but I would kind of classify it as the begin like, it's been a while, you know? Like, it's Yeah. Yeah.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, but I've gotten so much out of the community. I mean, I know we've talked before about, you know, my collective, we had a radio show where we would have different conversations and feature guest DJs and stuff, but also like I made some really lifelong connections through the Oroko community performing with like Phantom Wizard, who's up in Amsterdam as well.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Yeah, yeah, you said that. So cool. Yeah.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: But something I'm really curious about is like you have this community right that is spread across the entire world. You said 150, over 150 different cities. Like, what holds this community together, despite having that like geographic distance?

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Well, I do think that's why the radio is so important and such a big part of what we do and what we are, because, you know, I do feel… what I've heard a lot from residents, they would tap into other shows and kind of find, like, like-minded people, or sounds that they've never heard before, and they're not scared to reach out, because you're all part of this platform. Whereas I think for one DJ, if you see another DJ playing a cool set, maybe there's a little bit of a... A stop, like, from being nervous, or shy, or not really sure how to connect, or… I don't know, or maybe you just end up in the DMs, because, you know, people may not see it, or they think, oh, I don't know you, maybe I would… any given reason.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: And so I do feel like, excuse me, having this platform kind of takes away that barrier, takes away that wall. It's like, oh, sure, I'll write this person, because we're both an Oroko resident. So I do really feel like it's easier to talk to each other and stay in connection with each other, because we're all doing the same thing. We all have this show.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: And I think we push it a lot as well. Like anytime anybody would ask me anything, I remember one person not having recording for that week or for that month and they were like, "yo, I can't record this month because I don't have a studio." And I'll say like, "oh, of course, that's no problem. Thanks for letting me know. But if you do want to record, hey, here's this and this person in your city," or let's say they're traveling. And they're like, "yo, I can't record because this month I'm there and there." "Well, there's this and this and this person there, so maybe connect with them." So also, like, being, like, proactive and really, like, trying to not push that, but nurture it maybe, I think really helped.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: And I think, also, the way that we select the people, because obviously we do have to say no to people, you know, when they apply. I think the way that we select helps a lot, too. I do feel like it's all creative people that want to collaborate. There might be someone there who really just wants to play their show, it's for them, they want to make themselves big, and there's nothing wrong with that. If that's your, you know, the road you're on right now, that's the road you're on. But I do feel like you know, that's why we're interested in why people want to become a resident. We asked that question in our application as well. So I think having like-minded people and really, like pushing slash nurturing those connections throughout, not just at the start. "Hey, y'all can talk to each other," but really throughout at these touchpoints helps a lot, I think, yeah.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah. And it sounds like working in community, both here with Oroko, but outside of Oroko as well, is so foundational to how you work, right? I'm wondering why you might think that is.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Why I work like this?

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, yeah.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: It's just, it's always been me, like, that's always been me, like, I've... I'm autistic, so I was diagnosed super late in life, when I was 25 or 26, and I never really felt understood as a kid. And at some point, I also didn't really want to be understood anymore. But I did want friends, and so I would always move in every single group, like high school, I was friends with everybody, but I wasn't necessarily in that friend group that I would also go to the sleepover, but I would be friends with them, right? So… I feel like I'm I feel very comfortable In different crowds, because… I don't have to be this one specific person. I feel very layered and different sometimes and whatever, and I feel like I can always be myself in those groups, because I am all of those little things.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: I think this is such an interesting question because I never thought about it like this. So I'm hearing myself talk and I'm like, damn, that's like a revelation for myself. I think so. I think that has some something to do with it. And I don't know if it's autism or just me, but I hear like it's one of the, you know, traits that might like come from it as well.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: This sense of justice. And this sense of, like, so, since I'm young, if anybody bullies anyone, I will beat up that bully, because I have a big mouth, and I'm not small. So I will do that. And so, it's the same, I guess, with community. It's so important to me that people are seen, that people are heard, that people have a community. And I think that's just always been in me. So I'm very happy that I'm able to do this in work as well.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: And in any job I've ever had, I was always, for example, the… [Dutch] Like, the confidants, the confident… like, the person you go to, there's one person in the company that is, like, the person that you tell... Not HR, like, separate from HR. I don't know how it's…

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Like a confidant?

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Yeah, I suppose. So, it doesn't matter if I worked in a cultural space or not, I've always kind of had this, I suppose, so I do really think, like I'm so blessed. I feel so grateful that I'm able to work in this, you know?

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah. And then, like, on this sort of collaborative tip, like. What are… Are there specific processes that you think about that feel really essential to working together, when you're working with different groups of people?

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Yeah, like definitely communication always. I feel like that's a given, but it's not sometimes.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: I think you know. In Patta, I'm a producer, so I'm… we're… it's a clothing brand, so… and I do media production, so I'm in charge of all the photo shoots for all the campaign assets, everything, basically. So I need to, on one hand, wait for all the assets to come in, for all the items to come in, so that I can take pictures of them, and on the other hand, I have sales and social media ready for me to… oh, that's my hand. I saw an emoji, sorry. So on one hand, I have people waiting for those items, making those items, getting them to me, and on the other hand, I have people waiting for those assets. And so I'm always in the middle of those things. And if I don't communicate with all of that, it kind of falls apart. So I feel like that's kind of my job as well being in the middle of these things.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: So if let's say we had a collaboration with Somerset House in London. They asked me if I knew any residents, so then I need to look for the residents, but I need to be very open in communication, and I need to be super, like, on it, so I think communication is very important, as well as being, really knowing who you talk to.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: So… what I learned in social-cultural work studies, it's like you can also become a therapist and stuff. Every single person you talk to is different. So, when you talk to someone who has narcissistic traits, you would never give them like cognitive behavioral therapy, you would just go the Freudian way, put them on a couch, let them talk about themselves, basically, right? So, because otherwise, they don't feel in control. If you tell them, like, "hey, do da-da-da…"

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: So I feel like that's a lot the same when working with a community, like, who are you talking to? First, assess that, and then from there, base how you communicate on that. And then go on. And so I think that's very important to keep that. You need to also be consistent. I don't reply later than, like, 2 days for me is already a lot to reply. Because if I'm not consistent, they're not going to be consistent, and then there's no cohesion, right? So, I don't know, that's again kind of communication, I suppose, but yeah, really knowing who you talk to, being consistent, being transparent, I think people really value that.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: I think it's important for them to also be able to speak up then, and be themselves in the community, feel comfortable in the community. Feeling like you're able to speak up. Yeah.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah. Wow, that was an awesome, awesome answer.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Yeah, okay, good.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, and it's really interesting hearing too, like I'm tying it back to what you were talking about before about like Dutch culture and having like a desire for things to be a particular way.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: It's like existing in community we all, I feel like, want to build these spaces that people feel comfortable in, but sometimes being the one who is building community rather than just being in community means being the one to like do that hard work of like...

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Yeah.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: ...Being consistent, following up on time, all of these sort of things. So that's beautiful.

words: I'm curious about like what kind of social structures exist in the Oroko community like explicit structures that you all have to like support the social health, or like community health of the the residents, you know.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Yeah, so, as I mentioned, trying to… if somebody, for example, doesn't have a place… like, this is a very practical example, I would say. If somebody doesn't have a place to record, try to find, like, other spaces around that person, so that they have the support from somewhere else. Would that be an example of what you mean?

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, definitely.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Okay, so yeah, I definitely think things like that, but also, like I said, I need people to feel comfortable to email me. So, if you don't email me that you're gonna be late for a show because you have ADD, and you just didn't think about it, and you're scared, and now you're not gonna email me, and I email you saying, hey, you missed your deadline, and then you get even more scared, and you never email again, and then your show is gone. That's not how you can build a community.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: So, let's say somebody… if… you get 3 strikes to not send in your show. Every time you don't send it, I send you an email, "hey, you missed your show, we'd still love to play it," that's also a way I speak. I say, like, "we'd still love to play your show," instead of saying, like "send it in, we need it," or so. It's more like, "hey, yo, I want to hear it." And that kind of motivates people, I've noticed, to still send in a show, then, that we can use for the next week, which helps us, because people will be late for their shows, which means an empty slot, and then I have a new one from last week, right? So, kind of knowing what I need in the technical side also kind of influences our communication around those topics.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: And I think… There was someone who, yeah, unfortunately, he was just going through a really hard time. He didn't have equipment anymore, to record anything. No funds to do anything, and… I felt so bad, because I really wanted to help, you know? Like, I almost sent, like, my own money, but then I realized, like, I can't, because if I do that for one person, then it's gonna have a domino effect, like, I just can't do that. I need to make sure that I don't, because… You know, like, yeah, I just can't do that. But for example, what I then looked for is, okay, what opportunity is coming up that we can give this person that's really in need that we can push this person to, for example. And I was just going through all of our projects, and I was able to find something. It was, like, a curated thing. Then I was able to, like… get them, like... to move the deadline, to give it, like, a little bit of time. I said, like, if we can move this project, I have an amazing person, da-da-da. And then in that time frame, at some point, he emailed me, and he was like, yo, I was able to get a phone, I can make a show again. Mind you, a mobile phone. And he made an entire show on this mobile phone and was able to make some money through it because we did this.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: So, I think really looking for solutions in these moments, because we don't have, like, a funding structure for, or, like, a payment thing, because we are not-for-profit. So I think, like, I try to build, like... Yeah, like… those… how did you call it? Community health structure? I guess I try to build it like that, kind of just trying to find solutions and such, and...

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Let's say we need to… do an artwork. Like, right now, we're in the process of getting someone's artwork, like, having someone do artwork for new merchandise. I know someone who's going through a bit of a difficult time. They happen to be a graphic designer. There's a list of 3 people. I tend to then like choose the the that person who might be struggling a little bit so I don't know I guess.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: But then I only know they're struggling, I guess, because they felt comfortable telling me that, right? So then again, you go to the core of it all, which is making sure that you provide an open clear, communicative space for people to really also kind of tell you what they need. So, unfortunately, because we're not-for-profit, we're not able to, like, just give people fees or anything like that. But I hope that in the opportunities that we give people, and, like, by just kind of understanding the social structure in everything, I suppose. I hope that we can still support in those ways.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah. So you just mentioned that Oroko is structured as a not-for-profit. Can you speak a little bit about that decision, and like, what kind of economic practices work in the community, right?

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Yeah, so basically, it started as a Ghanaian entity only, but then we noticed that it was really hard to get fundings and grants, and because of all of the processing fees and, like, just a lot of bureaucratic headache, basically. And so, we also started a UK entity. This is a CIC, which is a community... Community… how can I forget? You know when you have a blackout sometimes?

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, like you said you say the word so many times, you forget.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Exactly. Community interest company. Which means that you can make profit, but you need to back it up by saying, this is why we made that profit, and this is what we'll do with that profit. So the whole time, anytime we make money, some money goes into the company, and we make sure that with that, for example, we're running this radio broadcast, right? This is also one of the reasons why we had to stop for a while and put this hiatus, start this hiatus. Because we simply did not have money to keep doing the radio.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: And one thing we wanted to be very wary of is working with brands who just want to show that they've been to Africa. Not even naming a country, Africa, right? Africa. And so, I think that was one of the, like, core values... Is one of the core values of Oroko, that we do not want to work with brands who only use the continent and don't want to support and nourish and, you know, make it flourish.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: And so we have done, for example, we've done… when we do Adidas, for example, right? We do that because… We did that because, first of all, it's a great budget. With that budget, we can put everything back in the community. We can do, like, in-depth workshops. If we don't have a lot of money, we can't even do these workshops. We were able to build a sound system. We were able to bring people from Africa. So, most of the time when we do brand deals, the number one motivation is so that we can bring people from from Accra, from Nairobi, from wherever. Because otherwise we're not able to do that, and…

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: Yeah, we've just noticed that there are some brands who are still good, like Jagermeister. They're a brand who is genuinely interested in the creativity, the artistry of an artist, in all of the layers of that artist, right? So… I think there are specific brands who you might think is just this brand. But beneath the surface, they're more culturally aware, I suppose.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: So yeah, we never wanted to be rich. And I think it's crazy because I got some DMs. I get some DMs sometimes like "yo, bring me to, bring me to the UK, bring me on a EU tour, can, can I get paid for a show?" And I'm like "I'm broke, we're broke, like I don't have, I'm poor. I don't know what you think we are, but Oroko Radio is a not-for-profit," you know. So I think for some people they might think... And that's also why we're wary of doing stuff with big brands, people will just think like you're walking around... Around with, like, so much revenue and so much everything, but we don't we don't have that. You know, so we want to be very wary of that.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: And at the same time, now… we are noticing, to be able to run a not-for-profit to be able to run a broadcast, we need money. And we cannot only rely on funding. The last two years, the funding landscape has drastically changed. It became really, really bad, and so we need to do that, and so we have some merchandise, for example. We have a Patreon, but that doesn't cover the costs, right? We have a three-person team. One of the reasons is also money. We don't have money to pay other people, so we just do everything ourselves, which means that we get overworked, right? So…

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: we've always kind of had this structure of, we're just doing this so that we can have a radio station, so that people can be on this radio station. And now we're trying to make it a little bit more sustainable, as in, okay, we need to also think about ourselves, because we can't run a station if we're overworked, don't have money, and can't really run it, so…

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: I think right now, what we're trying to do is pivot a little bit more to these brand partnerships, conscious brand partnerships, maybe find museums, institutions, you know, more like that. And yeah, try to make some revenue for the first time, so that we can, again, just make this radio work, right? Not to put money in our own pockets, for sure. Like, I don't foresee myself having like, a salary in the next I don't know how long, but I'm okay with that, yeah.

words: Mhmm. words: And, right now, it's a little bit different, because I became director as well. So, like, last year... speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: So, Doghouse, for example, he was volunteering because I had some calls with him, he just asked me some questions about, like, community radio. speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: So we always, whenever we have something to do, artwork, any job that we have, we look in our community, like, first people. So, any kind of job that we have, it goes to a resident most of the time, or someone in our community. So in that way, definitely, we always try to… try to put them on, or involve them.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: And so right now, because we're also restructuring and making… so… You're actually the first person I'm telling this... I guess I can say it in here. We're about to launch, like, something called Oroko Studios, where we, under that banner, we will now start doing our events, our, our, our, anything, really. Our workshops, our, our visual content, documentaries. There's a documentary coming out in about 2 months as well.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: And so… in that thing, so me, Kike, and Elinam are the directors, the overseeing, and then… Kike is a CEO with the overall, like feel. She's really the one who came up with the name, with the logo, you know, so it's good to have that one person who embodies Oroko. And I'm the COO, because I'm all about operations and just making sure things go smooth, and Elinam will be more production, so very much on the ground, global expansion and stuff like that.

speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: And it's very interesting because we just finalized that yesterday, actually, and Kike was talking about maybe being creative director and things, and then all of a sudden she was like, "you know what? I kind of feel like my… it may be, like, a CEO, but I don't know," and then me and Elinam both were like, "no, that's you, like, take the title." And I noticed it was the same for me. COO sounds so, like, big, why would we give ourselves this big title? But then they were like, no, give yourself the title. speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: But yeah, so right now. That's really how it's structured. It's just this small team of people, and whenever we have extra jobs, we look within our community, mostly residents. speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Congratulations. That's a huge evolution and change. You know I'm really excited.

words: It's exciting! Yeah, because I'm really hoping with this, you know, we can… I don't want to say this, but, like, make some money so that we can do all the things we want to do.

words: My dad, like, my dad is such a communist, like, very much, like, to the bone, like. My great… my family is from the CPN, which is the Communist Party of Holland. speaker: Jinan Vijent
words: And so… this is really something that we're trying to tell ourselves, you know, we're not gonna be this, like, for-profit company now, that's not what it means, it just means that we're able to sustain a thriving community, and we're able to just, like, do that in a very healthy, sensible way.
